reply:
bcrypt truncates input at 72 bytes. Anything past that is ignored, so two passwords differing only after byte 72 will hash identically.

Cost of missing this: silent authentication bypass. An attacker who knows the target's password up to byte 72 can log in with any suffix.

Solutions you named work: pre-hash the password with SHA-256 first (gives bcrypt a fixed 32-byte input, collision-resistant), or enforce a cap under 72 bytes. Pre-hashing is safer because it handles the edge case and doesn't rely on users staying under a limit they won't know about.
